subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which condition is thought to have been true of the early Earth's atmosphere before life began?
choices: High concentration of ozone
Little or no free oxygen
About 21% oxygen, as today
No carbon-containing gases
items.note: The early atmosphere was reducing, with little O₂ (and so no ozone layer, letting UV reach the surface). Oxygen built up later from photosynthesis.

choices: Organic molecules such as amino acids can form from inorganic gases
Living cells can arise spontaneously from simple organic molecules in water
RNA can copy itself without any enzymes
DNA was the first genetic material
items.note: It simulated early-Earth gases, water and lightning and produced amino acids — evidence for abiotic synthesis of carbon compounds, not for the origin of cells themselves.

items.stem: Why could the first cells not have formed by spontaneous generation in today's conditions?
choices: Today's oceans contain far too much salt for any membranes to form
Modern temperatures are too high for any organic molecule
Today's atmosphere lacks nitrogen for building amino acids
Organic molecules would be consumed by existing organisms or oxidised
items.note: Today, oxygen and living things destroy or use simple organic molecules before they can accumulate. Cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

items.stem: Which property of fatty acids made the formation of the first membranes possible?
choices: They are fully hydrophilic and dissolve easily in water
They are fully hydrophobic and sink to the bottom of the ocean
They are amphipathic, so they assemble into vesicles in water
They form hydrogen bonds with each other to make a solid layer
items.note: A hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail make fatty acids self-assemble into spherical bilayer vesicles, giving a separate internal compartment.

items.stem: RNA is a likely candidate for the first genetic material because it can:
choices: Form a stable double helix like DNA
Store information and act as a catalyst
Code for proteins without any ribosomes
Be made only inside living cells
items.note: Ribozymes show RNA can catalyse reactions, including forming peptide bonds, while also storing a base sequence that can be copied.

items.stem: LUCA (the last universal common ancestor) is best described as:
choices: The first cell that ever existed on Earth
A virus that infected all early cells
A single-celled eukaryote that later gave rise to all plants and animals
The most recent population from which all current life descends
items.note: LUCA is not the first life; other lineages existed and went extinct. All living organisms share its universal genetic code and features.

items.stem: Which evidence supports the idea that all living organisms share a common ancestor?
choices: All use the same genetic code with only minor variations
All have mitochondria to release energy from glucose in respiration
All are made of more than one type of cell
All reproduce sexually using gametes
items.note: The near-universal genetic code (and shared genes, ribosomes, ATP) points to a single common origin.

items.stem: Where might LUCA have lived, according to some evidence from genes shared by all bacteria and archaea?
choices: In surface rock pools with high oxygen
In the upper atmosphere
Near deep-sea hydrothermal vents
On land in dry soil
items.note: Genes shared by both domains suggest a heat-tolerant, anaerobic life near vents, with chemical energy and mineral catalysts available.

items.stem: Which of these is a challenge in explaining the origin of cells, rather than evidence that has been reproduced experimentally?
choices: The formation of amino acids from simple gases with an energy source
The formation of vesicles from fatty acids in water
The origin of a self-replicating molecule with a catalytic function
The synthesis of simple sugars from formaldehyde
items.note: Abiotic amino acids, vesicles and some sugars have been produced in the lab; how self-replication arose remains the key unsolved step.

items.stem: Approximate dating of LUCA to about 4 billion years ago is based mainly on:
choices: Fossils of LUCA cells found in ancient rocks from hydrothermal vents
Radioactive dating of the RNA found in modern cells
Counting the layers in stromatolites from that time
Molecular clock estimates from differences in shared gene sequences
items.note: Molecular clocks use mutation rates in shared genes, calibrated against fossils and geology. No fossil of LUCA exists.

items.stem: Cells need a membrane before they can become units of natural selection because a membrane:
choices: Makes the cell large enough to see under a microscope
Keeps a cell's own molecules together, so their products benefit that cell
Stops all mutations happening in the genetic material
Lets every molecule pass freely in and out, so nutrients are never limiting
items.note: Compartmentalisation keeps enzymes, RNA and their products together, so a better variant benefits its own vesicle and can be selected.

items.stem: Outline the evidence from the Miller–Urey experiment for the origin of carbon compounds on Earth.
markscheme: Simulated early atmosphere: methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water vapour (1)
Electric sparks simulated lightning as an energy source (1)
Amino acids/organic compounds formed (after about a week) (1)
Shows carbon compounds could form without living organisms (abiotically) (1)
items.tactic: Outline experiments as: set-up → result → what it shows.

items.stem: Explain the importance of vesicle formation in the origin of cells.
markscheme: Fatty acids/phospholipids spontaneously form vesicles in water (1)
Vesicles separate internal contents from the surroundings (1)
Keeps molecules (e.g. RNA) together so they can interact (1)
items.tactic: Link each structural event to the advantage it gives.

items.stem: Describe the main stages thought to be needed for the origin of the first cells.
markscheme: Synthesis of simple organic molecules (e.g. amino acids, nucleotides) (1)
Formation of self-replicating molecules (e.g. RNA) to allow inheritance (1)
Linking these with a source of energy / metabolism (1)
items.tactic: Sequence questions: give steps in order and name what each step makes possible.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) In an invented laboratory test of early-Earth chemistry, mixtures of gases were exposed to sparks for 7 days. Mass of amino acids formed (mg): Mixture A (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O) 12.0; Mixture B (CO₂, N₂, H₂O) 0.8; Mixture C (CO₂, N₂, H₂O, plus iron sulfide mineral) 3.5.
(a) Calculate how many times more amino acids formed in A than in B. (b) Suggest why mixture A gave the highest yield. (c) Suggest what the result for mixture C indicates about possible sites for the origin of life.
markscheme: (b) Mixture A is reducing / contains hydrogen-rich gases so carbon compounds form more easily (1)
(c) Mineral catalysts increased the yield compared with B (3.5 vs 0.8 mg) (1)
This supports sites rich in minerals, such as hydrothermal vents (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
